patterns.formal: Formal you: pan / pani + 3rd person verb
patterns.speaker: Gender follows the speaker

lines.speaker: Tomek
lines.pl: Dzień dobry, pani|pani_title Krystyno|krystyno! Jak się pani|pani_you miewa|miewa?
lines.en: Good morning, Mrs. Krystyna! How are you keeping?

lines.speaker: Krystyna
lines.pl: Dzień dobry, panie|panie Tomku|tomku. Dziękuję, nie narzekam|narzekam. A pan|pan?
lines.en: Good morning, Tomek. Thanks, I can’t complain. And you?

lines.speaker: Tomek
lines.pl: Wszystko dobrze. Pozwoli|pozwoli pani, że przedstawię|przedstawie: to Ania, moja koleżanka|kolezanka z pracy|pracy.
lines.en: All good. Allow me to introduce Ania, a colleague from work.

lines.speaker: Krystyna
lines.pl: Bardzo mi|mi miło. Krystyna Nowak. Pani|pani_ania też tu mieszka|mieszka?
lines.en: Very nice to meet you. Krystyna Nowak. Do you live here too?

lines.speaker: Ania
lines.pl: Nie, jestem tylko w odwiedzinach|odwiedzinach. Słyszałam|slyszalam, że ma pani najpiękniejszy|najpiekniejszy balkon w całym bloku|bloku.
lines.en: No, I’m just visiting. I heard you have the most beautiful balcony in the whole building.

lines.speaker: Krystyna
lines.pl: Och, Tomek przesadza|przesadza! Ale proszę, mówcie|mowcie mi Krystyna. Przejdziemy|przejdziemy na ty|ty?
lines.en: Oh, Tomek exaggerates! But please, call me Krystyna. Shall we use first names?

lines.speaker: Tomek
lines.pl: Bardzo chętnie, Krystyno|krystyno2. To my już lecimy|lecimy. Miłego|milego dnia|dnia!
lines.en: Gladly, Krystyna. We’ll be off, then. Have a nice day!

pani_title.gloss: Mrs., madam; formal “you” to a woman
pani_title.tags: noun · feminine · vocative singular (same form as nominative)
pani_title.why: Pani plus a first name is the usual polite way to address someone you know, such as a neighbor. Pani plus surname is rare in direct address. Both words are in the vocative; pani just looks the same as the nominative.
pani_title.compare: To a man: panie Tomku (next line).

krystyno.why: Feminine nouns in -a take -o in the vocative: Krystyna → Krystyno, Anna → Anno. In casual speech many people use the nominative with a bare first name, but after pani the vocative is the norm.
krystyno.compare: Diminutives in -ia take -u instead: Ania → Aniu.

pani_you.why: Formal “you” is grammatically a noun, so the verb is third person: jak się pani miewa, literally “how does madam fare.” The informal equivalent is jak się masz?
pani_you.compare: To a man: Jak się pan miewa?

miewa.gloss: to have (from time to time); to be keeping (well)
miewa.tags: verb · imperfective · iterative · present · 3rd person singular
miewa.why: Miewać is the iterative counterpart of mieć, “to have.” Jak się pani miewa is a slightly more formal, somewhat old-fashioned version of jak się pani ma. The verb is third person because it agrees with pani.

panie.gloss: Mr., sir; formal “you” to a man
parts: vocative -e (the i marks n softened to ń)
panie.why: Unlike pani, pan has a distinct vocative: panie. Krystyna answers at the same level of politeness Tomek used with her: title plus first name.
panie.compare: Nominative: pan, as in A pan? at the end of this line.

tomku.why: The e of the suffix -ek is a fleeting vowel: it appears only in the nominative singular (Tomek, but Tomka, Tomkowi). Nouns in -ek take -u in the vocative: Tomku, Marku, Jacku.
tomku.history: Tomek is the usual short form of Tomasz, from Greek Thōmas, from Aramaic for “twin.”

narzekam.why: Nie narzekam, “I can’t complain,” is a stock reply to “how are you,” a notch more modest than dobrze.

pan.why: A pan? means “And you?” to a man. When you’re on formal terms, “you” is pan or pani, never ty.

you.m: People will ask you: A pan?
you.f: People will ask you: A pani?

pozwoli.why: Pozwoli pani, że przedstawię… is a set phrase for introductions. The verb is third person because it agrees with pani.

przedstawie.tags: verb · perfective · non-past (future meaning) · 1st person singular
parts: 1st sg. ending -ę (the i marks w softened)
przedstawie.why: A perfective verb in its present-tense form refers to the future: “(allow me that) I’ll introduce.” The parts are close to literal: przed, “in front of,” plus stawić, “to place.”

kolezanka.why: Built on kolega with the feminine suffix -anka. Adding z pracy makes it clear she’s a colleague and not a personal friend.
kolezanka.compare: A male colleague: mój kolega z pracy.

pracy.why: Z meaning “from” takes the genitive: z pracy, z Polski. With the instrumental, z means “with”: z Tomkiem.

mi.why: Polish says “it’s pleasant to me”: bardzo mi miło. Mi is the short dative of ja; the full form mnie is used for emphasis and after prepositions.
mi.compare: Same pattern: zimno mi, “I’m cold”; przykro mi, “I’m sorry.”

pani_ania.why: Krystyna has only just met Ania, so she uses pani even though Ania is much younger. Between adults, formality depends on how well you know each other.
pani_ania.compare: To a man: Pan też tu mieszka?

you.m: Someone you’ve just met would ask: Pan też tu mieszka?
you.f: Someone you’ve just met would ask: Pani też tu mieszka?

parts: stem; 3rd person sg. has no ending
mieszka.why: Third person because it agrees with pani. To a friend you’d say mieszkasz.

odwiedzinach.why: Odwiedziny exists only in the plural, even for a single visit, much like English “scissors.” Być w odwiedzinach means “to be visiting.”

slyszalam.tags: verb · imperfective · past · 1st person singular · feminine
slyszalam.why: Ania is talking about herself, so the feminine ending -a. As in chcieć → chciała, the e of słyszeć alternates with a before the past suffix.

you.f: You would say: słyszałam, as Ania does.

parts: comparative suffix -ejsz- (the i marks n softened to ń)
najpiekniejszy.why: The superlative is the comparative (piękniejszy, “more beautiful”) with naj- in front. It’s masculine to agree with balkon; after ma it’s accusative, which for masculine inanimate nouns looks like the nominative.

bloku.why: W + locative. Masculine and neuter nouns whose stem ends in k, g or ch take -u in the locative instead of -e: w bloku, w parku, na brzegu, w dachu.
bloku.history: Blok is the everyday word for an apartment building, especially the post-war prefabricated kind.

przesadza.why: Krystyna is talking about Tomek, so the verb is third person. Prze- often adds “too much”: przesadzać, przepłacić “to overpay,” przejeść się “to overeat.”
przesadza.history: Przesadzać also means “to transplant” a plant; sadzić is “to plant.”

mowcie.why: Krystyna is speaking to both of them, so she uses the plural imperative. Once people are on first-name terms, the plural of ty is wy.
mowcie.compare: To one person: Mów mi Krystyna.

przejdziemy.tags: verb · perfective · non-past (future meaning) · 1st person plural
parts: root of iść (id-), d softened to dź
przejdziemy.why: Przejść na ty, literally “to cross over to ty,” means agreeing to use first names. By custom the older or more senior person suggests it, as Krystyna does here.

ty.tags: pronoun · used here as a noun
ty.why: In na ty, the pronoun stands for the informal relationship itself. The opposite is being na pan or na pani.

krystyno2.why: Now that they’re on first-name terms, Tomek drops pani and uses her name on its own, still in the vocative.
krystyno2.compare: Line 1, before the switch: pani Krystyno.

lecimy.why: Literally “we’re flying.” In casual speech it means “we’re off, we have to go.”

milego.why: Miłego dnia is short for życzę miłego dnia, “I wish you a nice day.” Życzyć takes the genitive, and the case stays even when the verb is dropped.

parts: stem: fleeting e lost, d + soft ń
dnia.why: Genitive because of the unspoken życzę. The e of dzień is a fleeting vowel, so the other forms are built on dń-, spelled dni before a vowel: dnia, dniu.
dnia.history: The same word hides in tydzień, “week” (see Plany na sobotę).

exercises.prompt: Greet Mrs. Barbara politely: Dzień dobry, pani ___!
exercises.explain: Feminine names in -a take -o in the vocative, like Krystyna → Krystyno.
exercises.hint: How did Tomek address Krystyna in the first line?

exercises.explain: Like Tomek → Tomku: the fleeting e drops and the vocative ending is -u.
exercises.hint: What happened to the e when Tomek became Tomku?

exercises.explain: Ciekawy forms its comparative with plain -szy (ciekawszy), so the superlative is naj + ciekaw + sz + y.
exercises.hint: Start from the comparative ciekawszy. Which piece turns it into a superlative?

explain.m: The masculine has no agreement ending, and an e is inserted before the person marker: widział + e + m. As in słyszeć → słyszał, the e of widzieć alternates with a.
explain.f: Built like Ania’s słyszałam: widzia + ł + a + m.

exercises.hint: Check the learner setting at the top, and remember what happens to the e in słyszeć → słyszałam.

exercises.prompt: Tell two friends: “Write to me!” ___ do mnie! (pisać)
exercises.explain: Imperative stem plus -cie for the plural: piszcie, like mówcie.
exercises.hint: Krystyna says mówcie to two people. Find the imperative stem of pisać and add the same ending.
